- How to Teach Accounting Effectively


Teaching accounting is more than preparing students to crunch numbers. Math skills and tech fundamentals remain important, but the profession is increasingly moving toward high-level client support in areas such as financial planning and risk management.


That evolution changes what effective instruction looks like. Engaging lessons and scenario-based exercises encourage students to think critically and exercise problem-solving skills. Hands-on experience with industry tools like QuickBooks is also valuable in helping students build the skills they’ll need on the job.


Learn how to effectively teach accounting and support learners at all levels. These tips cover how to prep and how to keep students engaged.


## **Key Points**


- The accounting industry is changing. Educators play a key role in preparing future accountants for what the job looks like in practice today.
- Interactive lesson formats, real-world scenarios, case studies, and accounting software can all help concepts stick.
- Effective instruction looks different across formats and stages of learning.
- Applied accounting projects test understanding in ways quizzes and exams can’t.


## **Designing Engaging Lessons and Activities**


The[US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/accountants-and-auditors.htm#tab-1) projects a 5% increase in accounting employment through 2035, although it’s worth noting that many of those opening are driven by retirements or industry churn. But the[American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/news/article/accounting-firms-report-strong-hiring-outlook-aicpa-report-finds) finds that the number of students earning a bachelor’s or master’s in accounting dropped 6.6% in 2023-24.


Fewer students are choosing the field, meaning that engaging instruction helps students stay with the material and build the skills employers are hiring for. To make lessons stick, teach accounting using a mix of interactive formats:


- **Real-world case studies:** Create lessons based on real business data so students can apply what they’ve learned. Push them to think critically about each case study and discuss what they’d do differently. Get them to question the data they’re analyzing and come up with creative solutions to specific problems.
- **Games:** Interactive tools like[AICPA’s Bank On It](https://www.thiswaytocpa.com/program/bankonit) reinforce fundamental accounting knowledge and give them a feel for workplace scenarios.
- **Collaborative problem-solving exercises:** Accounting isn’t a solo profession. Break students into small groups to work together on applied projects and case studies. Encourage them to help one another so nobody falls behind.
- **Visuals and video:** Lectures still work, but pairing them with slides, animations, and short videos helps reach students who learn visually.
- **Other hands-on activities:** Include practical exercises in your lessons, like mock bookkeeping activities or financial statement analysis scenarios. You could also use single-step flashcards to reinforce concepts.
- **Journal entry prompts:** Reflection prompts build critical thinking and give students space to work through accounting concepts on their own terms.


Looking to make teaching accounting or finance fun and engaging for all learners?[Intuit for Education](https://www.intuit.com/solutions/education/) offers free curriculum and real-world tools to do just that.


### **Using Real-World Scenarios to Reinforce Concepts**


Real-world scenarios are among the most effective ways to[teach financial literacy](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/teaching-financial-literacy/) or accounting. Students tend to engage more deeply when they work through actual problems, and the context helps the concepts stick.


To bring real-world situations into the classroom, you might have students:


- **Run a mock business.** Put students in small groups and have them build a business from scratch, tracking revenue and expenses over a set period. Get them to log all transactions and create digital financial statements and records to help them get used to working in a virtual environment.
- **Analyze real public company financials.** Understanding financial statements is key to making informed decisions and identifying business risk and opportunity. Have students analyze real statements to assess a company’s financial performance and health. Encourage them to interpret changes to the data over time. Adjusting a few entries ahead of time is a useful way to test whether they can catch errors and clean up the books.
- **Work through tax filing scenarios.** Teach students to recognize tax breaks, liabilities, and the forms behind each. Pair those lessons with hands-on practice in tax and accounting software like QuickBooks, since 53% of accounting professionals in[Intuit’s 2026 Accountant Technology Survey](https://www.firmofthefuture.com/news/accountant-tech-survey-2026/) said software and technology certifications improve entry-level hiring prospects.


## **Assessment Strategies That Measure Real Understanding**


Teaching accounting effectively involves knowing when (and how) to assess your students’ understanding of the materials. A mix of formats gives you the clearest picture:


- **Quick quizzes, exit tickets, journal entries:** These are low-stakes formative checks that test comprehension. You might use them after introducing a complex concept or wrapping up a module.
- **Summative exams:** Best for end-of-term or end-of-unit assessment, these push students to apply what they’ve learned rather than recall it.
- **Applied projects:** These test critical thinking and problem-solving skills in a realistic context. For example, you might have students prepare a comprehensive set of financial statements for a fictional client. Smaller projects every few weeks work well. You might save larger ones for key milestones.


Use assessment data to inform your lesson plans and set goals for improvement. Expect to adjust your testing frequency until you find the right cadence. Test too often, and you could overwhelm your students or lose sight of where to course-correct.


Students learn at different paces and in different ways. When standard assessments aren’t providing you a clear read, try alternative formats like:


- Written essays
- 1-on-1 interviews
- Reflective journal entries
- Presentations or smaller projects (solo or group)
- Structured accounting activities or scenarios
- Self-evaluations and peer evaluations


To protect academic integrity, you could layer in a few safeguards, such as:


- Using different assessment types, including low-stakes checks
- Setting clear expectations for your students
- Breaking larger projects or assignments into more manageable chunks
- Positioning proctors strategically, such as one in the back and one circulating the classroom
- Aiming for a 1:35 proctor-to-student ratio on exam day
- Setting up continuous audio and video monitoring for online or computer-based exams


## **Technology and Tools for Teaching Accounting**


According to[Intuit’s](https://www.firmofthefuture.com/news/accountant-tech-survey-2026/) Accountant Technology Survey, the average accounting firm uses 10 software programs or apps in day-to-day operations. Some use even more than that. Among the[most common accounting tools](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/best-ai-accounting-software-tools/) are:


- QuickBooks with[Intuit Intelligence](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/intuit-intelligence/) for automated categorization, insights, and reporting
- Xero for bank reconciliations, real-time reporting, and invoicing
- Zoho Books for accounting workflow automation, inventory, and multi-currency
- Vic.ai for invoice capture, approvals, and spend visibility
- Dext for receipt capture, extraction, integrations, and pre-accounting workflows
- BILL for vendor payments, invoice workflows, approvals
- Kahoot! for gamification of accounting concepts


Teaching accounting, especially at the college level, means making sure your students are familiar with these tools. They don’t need to master every platform, but hands-on exposure to a few goes a long way.


In your lessons, include spreadsheet-based exercises like building budgets and reconciling accounts. Build in spreadsheet exercises in Excel or Google Sheets, like constructing budgets and reconciling accounts, and use interactive tools like Mentimeter for polling and live demos.


A reusable resource library also pays off over time. Keep a working set of:


- Problem sets
- Worked solutions
- Slide templates and PowerPoint decks
- Short video walkthroughs

## **Supporting Learners at Every Level**


Teaching accounting looks different at the undergraduate and graduate levels, and different again for students coming in with no finance background. The job is to meet students where they are without leaving behind those who are ahead or holding back those who are behind.


A few strategies for supporting a mixed classroom:


- **Scaffolding:** Break your accounting content into distinct segments and offer more hands-on direction early on. As students build confidence, pull back your involvement until they can work independently.


- **Tiered assignments:** Split your students into groups based on skill level. Give struggling students a task that reinforces their understanding. Challenge more advanced learners with an activity that extends what they know. You can use the same materials for both groups, but resources and outcomes may vary based on student readiness.
- **Remediation:** If most of the class is stuck on a foundational concept like numeracy, reteach it. When only a few students are struggling, offer targeted support outside of class.
- **Extension tasks:** If you have students with a bookkeeping or accounting background, you might need to challenge them more. The same goes for those who appear bored in class or who always receive top marks. Introduce personalized content or tasks requiring higher critical thinking or problem-solving skills.
- **Peer tutoring:** In larger classrooms especially, consider pairing more advanced students with those who need extra support. This can be effective for managing varied learning paces.


Regular assessments, even quick quizzes, can keep you in tune with what’s going on in the classroom. Student feedback is worth collecting, too, and keeping it anonymous encourages more candid responses. You can use the information you collect to adjust your approach as you go.


### **Adapting Instruction for Online, Hybrid, and Large-Section Formats**


As of 2024, 53.8% of college students took at least one online course, according to the[US Department of Education](https://nces.ed.gov/ipeds/trendgenerator/app/answer/2/42) . Even experienced instructors often need to redesign their courses when the delivery format changes.


Keep these tips in mind if you’re going from in-person to hybrid or fully remote:


- Design lessons for the format from the start, with recorded lectures, digital problem sets, and discussion boards built in.
- Set clear office hours and make it easy for students to reach you with questions or feedback.
- Define learning goals up front, and revise any that worked in person but don’t translate online.
- Confirm students have the equipment and connectivity they need.
- Scaffold your content into distinct lessons and modules with clear directions and pathways.
- Keep hands-on activities and group problem-solving in person where possible.
- Be aware of your students’ bandwidth for online learning. Plan your courses around weekly learning goals.
- Use technology that allows for real-time interaction or meetings. This includes features like videoconferencing and live chat.
- Provide both regular assessments and opportunities for self-assessments. For important exams, you may need to use proctoring software like Examity to protect academic integrity.


For multi-section courses or larger cohorts:


- Standardize course materials across sections.
- Coordinate with other accounting instructors to keep teaching consistent.
- Train teaching assistants to help with grading, exam proctoring, and weekly check-ins.
- Use course management tools like CourseWorks to manage courses or deliver feedback via audio and video messages.
- Set up regular reminders regarding upcoming assignments or deadlines.
- Encourage collaboration and open feedback.


## **FAQs**


###


You’ll generally need at least a master’s degree in accounting or a related field to teach accounting. Larger research universities may require a Doctor of Business Administration (DBA) or PhD. You’ll also need relevant skills, like business administration, accounting best practices, financial systems, and online course development. Prior accounting or online teaching experience is also often preferred.


###


A differentiated instruction approach works well for accounting. The learning outcome stays the same across the class, but the path each student takes is tailored to their strengths and weaknesses. Scaffold content into smaller segments so beginners can build confidence, and use tiered assignments to stretch advanced learners without overwhelming those who need more support.


###


Online learning has grown fast. In 2012, 25.5% of adult learners had taken a college course online. By 2024, that figure had more than doubled. To teach accounting online or in a hybrid setting, adapt your course structure. Create digital problem sets and discussion boards for your students. Provide timely feedback, but also encourage them to reach out whenever they need help. Leverage technology, too, as it can make managing online classes and assessments easier.
